questions.stem:
Argument: 'Students who study in the morning perform better academically.'
Which of the following WEAKENS this argument?

options.option_text: Studies show morning students have lower stress levels (strengthens — supports the argument)
A recent study found that academic performance depends primarily on total hours studied, not time of day (correct: undermines the argument by showing time-of-day is not the key factor ✓)
Many universities schedule important exams in the morning (irrelevant — exam timing doesn't affect when students study best)
Morning students tend to sleep earlier (supports — suggests disciplined routine)

questions.explanation: B is correct. To WEAKEN an argument, find a fact that undermines the causal link. The argument claims morning study → better performance. If performance depends on total hours, not time of day, then the time-of-day factor is not the cause — this directly weakens the argument.

questions.stem:
Conclusion: 'All politicians are corrupt.'
Which statement, if true, SUPPORTS this conclusion?

options.option_text: Many politicians have been found guilty of financial misconduct (weakly supports but uses 'many', not 'all')
Every politician investigated in the past decade was found to have engaged in corrupt practices (strongest support: if ALL investigated politicians were corrupt, it supports 'all are corrupt' ✓)
Some politicians have clean records (contradicts the 'all are corrupt' conclusion)
The political system lacks transparency (related but doesn't prove ALL politicians are corrupt)

questions.explanation: B is correct. The conclusion is 'ALL politicians are corrupt.' The supporting statement must be consistent with ALL being corrupt. Option B (every politician investigated = corrupt) most strongly supports this — though note that 'investigated' ≠ 'all politicians.' Of the options, B is the strongest support for the blanket conclusion.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Exercise reduces the risk of heart disease by 30%.'
Which is the STRONGEST assumption behind this statement?

options.option_text: All people who exercise will avoid heart disease (too absolute — the statement says 30% risk reduction, not elimination)
The 30% figure was derived from credible research on a sufficient sample size (correct: for a statistical claim to be valid, it must be based on proper research ✓)
People who don't exercise will definitely get heart disease (the statement doesn't imply this)
Heart disease is the only disease affected by exercise (too narrow — not implied by the statement)

questions.explanation: B is correct. An ASSUMPTION is an unstated premise that must be true for the statement to hold. For the 30% claim to be valid, it must be based on credible research — if the research is flawed, the claim collapses. This is the core assumption behind any statistical claim.

questions.stem:
'Since fewer people bought cars this quarter, the economy must be slowing down.'
What is the FLAW in this reasoning?

options.option_text: Car sales are the most important economic indicator (this assumption is itself not clearly stated)
The conclusion assumes that fewer car sales is the ONLY possible explanation for a slowing economy (wrong: this reverses the direction)
Fewer car sales could be due to other reasons (e.g., fuel prices, new car tech launches delayed) unrelated to the overall economy (correct: alternative explanations undermine the causal link ✓)
The economy always reflects car sales trends (this is a different flaw — generalisation)

questions.explanation: C is correct. The reasoning jumps from fewer car sales to a slowing economy without considering other causes. The FLAW = false causation / hasty generalisation. Fewer car sales might be due to supply chain issues, high prices, or consumer preference shifts — not necessarily economic slowdown. This is the classic 'correlation ≠ causation' error.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Most successful entrepreneurs dropped out of school.'
Can we conclude: 'Dropping out of school leads to success as an entrepreneur'?

options.option_text: Yes — the evidence clearly shows dropping out causes entrepreneurial success (wrong: this is hasty causation from correlation)
No — the statement describes a pattern among successful entrepreneurs but doesn't prove dropping out CAUSES success (correct: survivor bias and correlation vs causation ✓)
Yes — if most successful ones dropped out, then dropping out is the key factor (wrong: ignores that most dropouts are NOT successful)
Not enough information to decide (partially right but B is more specific about WHY)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Classic SURVIVOR BIAS and CORRELATION vs CAUSATION error. The statement observes a pattern among successful entrepreneurs but ignores: (1) most dropouts are NOT successful; (2) correlation doesn't prove causation. The conclusion that 'dropping out CAUSES success' is logically unwarranted.

questions.stem: Which LOGICAL FALLACY is committed: 'You can't trust Dr. Sharma's opinion on climate change because he drives a petrol car.'

options.option_text: False dilemma (false dilemma = presenting only two options when more exist)
Ad hominem (correct: attacking the person rather than their argument; irrelevant personal behaviour attacked ✓)
Straw man (straw man = misrepresenting someone's argument)
Circular reasoning (circular = using conclusion as premise)

questions.explanation: B is correct. AD HOMINEM fallacy = attacking the person instead of their argument. 'He drives a petrol car' is irrelevant to whether his climate change opinion is scientifically valid. Attacking personal behaviour to dismiss an argument is a classic ad hominem.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a STRONG argument for increasing the minimum wage?

options.option_text: Other countries have higher minimum wages (appeal to popularity/comparison; doesn't prove it would work here)
Increasing minimum wage will give workers more buying power, stimulating economic growth (correct: logical economic argument with clear mechanism — higher wages → more spending → growth ✓)
Workers deserve to be paid more for their efforts (emotional/moral appeal; not a logical economic argument)
Minimum wage hasn't been increased in years (age of the policy doesn't determine whether it should change)

questions.explanation: B is correct. A STRONG argument has: (1) a clear logical mechanism, (2) evidence or economic rationale, (3) relevance to the conclusion. B provides a clear economic mechanism (increased purchasing power → demand → growth). The other options rely on emotional appeals, comparisons, or non-logical bases.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'Reading improves vocabulary. Riya has an excellent vocabulary.'
Conclusion: 'Riya reads a lot.'
Is this conclusion valid?

options.option_text: Yes — reading improves vocabulary, so excellent vocabulary must come from reading (wrong: this reverses the logic)
No — the conclusion commits the fallacy of affirming the consequent (correct: 'reading → good vocab' doesn't mean 'good vocab → reading'; other causes exist ✓)
Yes — the relationship is bidirectional (wrong: the premise states only one direction)
Cannot be determined at all (partially right but B is more precise)

questions.explanation: B is correct. FALLACY OF AFFIRMING THE CONSEQUENT: If P then Q; Q is true; therefore P is true — INVALID. Reading (P) → good vocabulary (Q). Riya has good vocabulary (Q). Therefore Riya reads (P) = INVALID. Riya's vocabulary could come from other sources (conversations, word games, formal education).

questions.stem: Which is a WEAK argument against banning tobacco products?

options.option_text: Tobacco farming supports millions of livelihoods (relevant economic point — relatively strong argument)
My grandfather smoked for 70 years and lived to 90 (anecdotal evidence — weak argument; one case doesn't disprove population-level harm ✓)
Banning tobacco would create a black market, potentially worse outcomes (relevant public policy argument)
Adults have the right to make their own decisions about legal substances (relevant rights-based argument)

questions.explanation: B is correct. WEAK ARGUMENT. 'My grandfather smoked and lived to 90' is ANECDOTAL EVIDENCE — using a single personal example to counter population-level statistical evidence. One exception doesn't disprove the general rule. This is the 'hasty generalisation from a single case' fallacy.

questions.stem:
Statement: 'The population of City X has grown by 20% in 5 years.'
Conclusion: 'City X is becoming more prosperous.'
Is this inference valid?

options.option_text: Yes — population growth always indicates prosperity (wrong: population can grow due to migration driven by poverty, not prosperity)
No — population growth can occur for reasons other than prosperity (e.g., refugee influx, high birth rate) (correct: alternative causes make the inference uncertain ✓)
Yes — growing cities are always prosperous (wrong: too absolute and empirically false)
The statement provides no information for any inference (wrong: it does provide information; the question is whether the specific inference is valid)

questions.explanation: B is correct. Population growth does NOT necessarily indicate prosperity. Alternative explanations: high birth rate, migration from disaster areas, refugee influx, etc. The inference 'population growth → prosperity' is INVALID without additional data on economic indicators. This tests the ability to identify unwarranted inferences.
